original_value: In this study we performed a bibliometric analysis focusing on the general patterns of scientific publications about Cannabis, revealing their trends and limitations. Publications related to Cannabis, released from 1960 to 2017, were retrieved from the Scopus database using six search terms. The search term “Genetics” returned 53.4% of publications, while “forensic genetics” and “traceability” represented 2.3% and 0.1% of the publications, respectively. However, 43.1% of the studies were not directly related to Cannabis and, in some cases, Cannabis was just used as an example in the text. A significant increase in publications was observed after 2001, with most of the publications coming from Europe, followed by North America. Although the term Cannabis was found in the title, abstract, or keywords of 1284 publications, we detected a historical gap in studies on Cannabis. We expect that increasing interest in this issue and the rise of new biotechnological advances will lead to the development of new studies. This study will help scientists identify overall research needs, detect the scientific areas in evidence concerning Cannabis studies, and find excellent centers of investigation for scientific interchange and collaboration.

result.paraphrase: This study carried out a bibliometric review of scientific publications on Cannabis, examining broad publication patterns and their trends and limitations. Using six search terms, publications on Cannabis from 1960 to 2017 were retrieved from the Scopus database. The search term “Genetics” accounted for 53.4% of the publications, whereas “forensic genetics” and “traceability” made up 2.3% and 0.1%, respectively. However, 43.1% of the studies were not directly about Cannabis and, in some cases, Cannabis was only mentioned as an example in the text. A marked rise in publications was seen after 2001, and most papers originated in Europe, followed by North America. Although the word Cannabis appeared in the title, abstract, or keywords of 1284 publications, we identified a historical gap in Cannabis research. We expect that growing interest in this topic and the emergence of new biotechnological advances will foster new studies. This work will help scientists recognize overall research needs, identify active scientific areas in Cannabis studies, and locate excellent research centers for scientific exchange and collaboration.
